cost-budget.question: Which real I/O behaviors are omitted from the serial request model?

benchmark.title: An optimization needs two kinds of evidence
benchmark.note: A smaller live file count is useful only if the business answer remains correct. Historical storage remains separate.
benchmark.question: Why does an equal row count alone not prove that a rewrite preserved the answer?

incident.title: Repair fragmentation and preserve the answer
incident.note: The repair reduces current fragmentation. Retained history, rewrite resources and writer contention still need policies.
incident.question: Which costs remain after current-file consolidation succeeds?

recommendation.title: Connect a decision to evidence and its limits
recommendation.note: A defensible recommendation states what the local fixture supports and what could overturn the proposed design.
recommendation.question: What evidence would make you revise the recommended layout?

snapshots.title: Watch snapshots share a table’s history

scenes.title: A new batch does not erase yesterday
scenes.text: A report needs a consistent table state while ingestion keeps adding orders. Iceberg records successive states as snapshots. A snapshot describes a complete state using file references; it is not merely a bag of newly inserted rows.

scenes.title: Follow the parent links
scenes.text: In the default lesson fixture, the first batch creates snapshot one with forty rows. The second creates a state with eighty rows and names the first as its parent. The third state contains one hundred and twenty rows. Older immutable data files can be reused across these states.

scenes.title: Choose the state before querying
scenes.text: Reading an older snapshot selects its referenced inputs before the query runs. Keeping a snapshot identifier in a report is not enough on its own. Its metadata and data files must remain available. Run the lesson, follow the parent identifiers, then explain which state the current count describes.

scenes.title: One result can require much more work
scenes.text: A query returning one order does not prove that the reader inspected one row. Iceberg first uses metadata to choose candidate files. Rows in a kept file can still fail the row filter.

scenes.title: Test each file’s range
scenes.text: The fixture has three batches with disjoint order identifier ranges. For order one thousand and five, the ranges zero to thirty nine and two thousand to two thousand and thirty nine cannot match. Only the range one thousand to one thousand and thirty nine is kept.

scenes.title: Keep pruning and filtering separate
scenes.text: The remaining file contains forty candidate records, but only one row matches. These are different quantities. Selected file bytes are a sum of file sizes, not measured network traffic. Run the experiment with an Iceberg row filter, then change the target to a value outside every range.

atomic-pointer.title: Watch preparation become a published state

scenes.title: An uploaded file is not yet a committed change
scenes.text: A writer may finish uploading a new data file before it publishes the table change. If a reader treated every physical file as a member, it could read unfinished work. Iceberg readers instead follow the committed metadata state.

scenes.title: Publish one complete state
scenes.text: In this publication model, the catalog pointer initially names metadata version one, which references file A. File B can already exist. Preparing metadata version two still does not change the reader’s view. Successful publication changes the pointer so readers can resolve a state referencing both A and B.

scenes.title: Validate before replacing the pointer
scenes.text: Publication must check the writer’s expected starting state. If another writer has changed it, a blind replacement could lose that change. This lesson models the boundary, not a distributed catalog service. Run the real stale schema commit lesson to observe requirement validation in the local catalog.
